# The Subtle Principles of the Northern Section

<margin>Feeding on milk</margin>
When a child feeds at the breast of its dead mother, after a short while, it will look at her <margin>meaning the blinking of the eyes shows she is no longer there</margin>
and abandon her, rising up without looking at her any longer. This is because it does not recognize a kinship. The reason you loved your mother was <margin>the stiff body is no longer kin</margin>
<margin>if the form is not worth loving, then the essence is not worth loving</margin>
not because of her physical form, but because of that which animated her form. Those who die in battle are buried by others <margin>those who die in battle lack martial virtues, so one does not reward them with concubines</margin>
who do not sacrifice concubines to accompany them in death. A pregnant woman who miscarries <margin>repeatedly using the foot as a root</margin>
<margin>another metaphor: selecting concubines does not exhaust the wholeness of the form; this would be to impose a loss upon the supreme status</margin>
does not care for the fetus; all have abandoned the root. For the various consorts of the Son of Heaven, they do not trim their nails nor pierce their ears. When taking a wife, <margin>they are not engaged in official labor for fear of callousing their hands and feet, which would prevent them from fulfilling their duties in a new marriage</margin>
one remains on the outside and may not employ her, for if the form remains whole, it is still sufficient to move the <margin>those whose forms are whole are still sufficient to move others</margin>
intent.
Below the intent is the [true] reality.

<meta>Dechongfu (Virtue's Perfect Alignment)</meta>
<meta>Richuan Hall</meta>

<summary>This passage explores the nature of detachment and the preservation of the essential self over the physical form, using the metaphors of a nursing child and the requirements for palace consorts.</summary>
<keywords>Zhuangzi, Dechongfu, form, essence, detachment, nature</keywords>
